rows.title: Rainfall risk, fertility and development: evidence from farm settlements during the American demographic transition
rows.note: WALL 1 RE-CUT ON THE INSTRUMENT (RA ruling 2026-09-01, PI confirmation pending) -- and then CORRECTED AT FULL TEXT. I had routed this to C.5.a on its title, on the reasoning that rainfall risk varies and no instrument does. The full text splits: the HEADLINE effect (rainfall variance x farm/non-farm differential within counties over time) is C.5.a's, but Table 4 cols (5)-(6) interact rainfall variability with ACCESS TO FINANCIAL SERVICES, measured as banks per county and banks per farm, time-varying. That interaction IS Arm S's estimand: does access to a formal instrument reduce the use of children as a risk buffer? RETAINED in Arm S for that estimate; main effect cross-refs C.5.a. One study, two estimands -- do not route wholesale.

rows.title: Risk and Fertility: A Reply to Robinson
rows.note: RE-ROUTED AT FULL TEXT. Cain's reply is conceptual - it defends the coherence of treating children as insurance and reports no new estimate. AND IT RAISES A STRUCTURAL PROBLEM FOR WALL 1: Cain defines insurance as 'protection against the adverse economic consequences of a potentially threatening event', names disability, widowhood, depredation and floods alongside old age, and cites Nugent's old-age-security paper approvingly in support. The founding literature treats old-age security as ONE INSTANCE of the insurance motive, not a separable category - which is the axis Wall 1 cuts on. See the log.

rows.title: The No-Birth Bonus Scheme: The Use of Savings Accounts for Family Planning in South India
rows.note: RE-ROUTED AT FULL TEXT. The No-Birth Bonus Scheme pays into a savings account FOR EACH YEAR WITHOUT A BIRTH - the paper's own words, 'compensation for the loss incurred in forgoing additional children'. What varies is the PRICE OF A BIRTH; the savings account is the payment vehicle, not a change in the asset menu. Under the what-varies rule this is C.2.d. NOTE the design is otherwise good: a DiD over 18 tea estates, Type I (NBBS 1971) vs Type II (CLWS 1972) vs Type III (neither), CBR 1969-77; Type I 39.5 -> 25.4 against Type III 39.2 -> 33.0. The author's own verdict is cautious: rates were falling everywhere.
